newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hang Seng Bank sale seen too sensitive - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hang Seng Bank sale seen too sensitive - analysts.

text.p: Hong Kong's return to China has revived talk that Hang Seng Bank Ltd could find itself with a Chinese shareholder, but as one of the territory's largest banks, analysts said a deal would be too politically sensitive.

"Banking is the cornerstone of the whole economy. If China bought into Hang Seng Bank it would be called an encroachment on 'one country, two systems'," Stephen Thompson, chief analyst at Nikko Securities, said on Friday.
"It would generate heavy criticism from overseas that China is interfering in the financial system in Hong Kong," he said.
Hong Kong will be handed back to China on midnight of June 30 after 156 years of British colonial rule.
Under the "one country, two systems" formula, China has pledged that Hong Kong can keep its capitalist ways and enjoy a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the handover.

Shares of Hang Seng Bank, a unit of HSBC Holdings Plc and the second-largest locally incorporated bank in Hong Kong, rocketted HK$12.75 to end Friday at HK$109.50 (US$14.15) on speculation that a Chinese company could seek a stake in it.
The bank led the market's blue-chip Hang Seng Index up 4.47 percent or 647.87 points, its biggest point gain ever, to close at an all-time high of 15,154.36.

Hang Seng Bank released a statement through the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong saying it was not aware of any reason for the rise in its share price. The bank's shares had also surged on Thursday, gaining HK$4.50 to HK$96.75.
"The company is not aware of any reasons for such increases...There are no negotiations or agreements relating to intended acquisitions or realisations," it said.
HSBC Holdings also told Reuters on Friday that it had no plans to change its shareholding in Hang Seng Bank.
"Hang Seng is our long-term holding. We have no plan to change our holding in Hang Seng Bank," a spokeswoman said.
Richard Verin, head of equities trading at CS First Boston, said the rumour had been floated in the market from time to time for a long time. "It has always been denied," he said.
But he said the rumours did have some credibility since HSBC had two local banking operations through Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd, the territory's largest, and Hang Seng Bank.
"Hongkong Bank (HSBC) owns two very big banks here which are somewhat competitive. Just looking logically at the banking situation it might make sense to divest some of their holdings."
But Thompson said HSBC did not need the money.
"They have got bags of money and a 10 percent stake in Hang Seng Bank would be around HK$18 billion. That is a lot of beans and they have got plenty already," he said.
There has also been speculation HSBC may offer a piece of Hang Seng Bank to a Chinese partner in order to improve the group's prospects in the China market.
But one trader at a European brokerage noted HSBC Holdings was already authorised to operate in China and did not need a partner there, echoing recent comments made by Hongkong Bank.

"We have an excellent relationship with the Chinese government. They understand the bank, they respect the bank because we have demonstrated to everyone how successful we are and what sort of services we could provide to companies," executive director Vincent Cheng told Reuters in an interview.
He said a sale of HSBC's Hang Seng Bank stake had never been on the agenda and had not been discussed by the board.
"You can't force HSBC to give up Hang Seng Bank. It would prompt a crisis of confidence in Hong Kong," the European brokerage trader said.

"These guys are people that China needs and it wants to continue the prosperity of Hong Kong. Hang Seng Bank is one of the jewels in the crown and I find it hard to believe they would sell," he added. (US$1=HK$7.74)
